courses.title: Industrial Pharmacy and Good Manufacturing Practice
courses.description: Pharmaceutical manufacturing unit operations, solid dosage form production, sterile manufacturing, GMP and quality systems, validation, stability and the Nigerian pharmaceutical industry.

topics.title: Unit Operations in Pharmaceutical Manufacturing
topics.summary: Size reduction, mixing, granulation, drying, and particle properties.

material.heading: Size reduction and mixing
material.body: Unit operations are the fundamental steps of manufacturing. Size reduction (milling) increases surface area, improving dissolution and content uniformity: mills include hammer mills (impact — for brittle materials), ball mills (impact and attrition), fluid energy (jet) mills (micronisation to < 5 µm, no heat — for heat-sensitive drugs and inhalation products), and cutter mills. Particle size is measured by sieving, microscopy, laser diffraction and sedimentation. Mixing (blending) aims for content uniformity; segregation occurs with differences in particle size, density and shape. Mixers: tumbling (V-blender, double-cone), convective (ribbon blender) and high-shear mixers. Powder flow is assessed by angle of repose (< 30° excellent), Carr's compressibility index and Hausner ratio (< 1.25 good flow); glidants (colloidal silica) improve flow.
keyPoints: Angle of repose; Carr's index; Hausner ratio

material.heading: Granulation and drying
material.body: Granulation enlarges particles to improve flow, compressibility and uniformity and reduce dust. Wet granulation: mix powders, add binder solution (PVP, starch paste, HPMC), wet mass, screen, dry and size — robust but unsuitable for moisture- or heat-sensitive drugs. Dry granulation (slugging or roller compaction) suits moisture-sensitive drugs. Direct compression (blend and compress) is simplest and cheapest but requires good flow and compressibility (directly compressible excipients such as microcrystalline cellulose, spray-dried lactose). Drying removes solvent: tray dryers, fluidised bed dryers (efficient, uniform; also used for granulation and coating), spray dryers (liquid feeds to powder — heat-sensitive products because of short exposure) and freeze dryers (lyophilisation — sublimation of ice under vacuum for thermolabile biologicals and injections). Loss on drying measures residual moisture.

topics.title: Solid Dosage Form Production and Testing
topics.summary: Tablet compression, excipients, coating, capsules, defects and quality control tests.

material.heading: Tablets and capsules
material.body: Tablet excipients: diluents/fillers (lactose, microcrystalline cellulose, dibasic calcium phosphate, starch), binders (PVP, starch, HPMC), disintegrants (starch, croscarmellose, sodium starch glycolate, crospovidone — 'superdisintegrants'), lubricants (magnesium stearate — excess slows dissolution), glidants, and anti-adherents. Compression uses single-punch or rotary presses (upper and lower punches, die). Tablet defects: capping and lamination (air entrapment, excessive fines, too fast compression), picking and sticking (moisture, insufficient lubricant), mottling, weight variation (poor flow), and chipping. Coating: sugar coating (traditional, lengthy), film coating (HPMC-based — thin, efficient), and enteric coating (cellulose acetate phthalate, methacrylate polymers — dissolves in the intestine; protects acid-labile drugs or the stomach). Modified-release forms (matrix, reservoir, osmotic pumps) prolong action. Hard gelatin capsules are filled with powder or pellets; soft gelatin capsules hold liquids.

material.heading: Quality control tests
material.body: Pharmacopoeial tests for tablets: weight uniformity, content uniformity (for low-dose drugs), assay, hardness (crushing strength), friability (Roche friabilator — weight loss usually < 1%), disintegration (uncoated tablets typically within 15 minutes; film-coated 30 minutes; enteric-coated — no disintegration in acid for 2 hours then disintegration in buffer), and dissolution (USP apparatus 1 — basket; 2 — paddle; results compared with specifications and used to compare generics). Bioequivalence studies (AUC and Cmax 90% confidence intervals within 80–125%) demonstrate generic interchangeability. Substandard and falsified medicines are a major problem in Nigeria — quality control laboratories (NAFDAC, manufacturers), GMP compliance and pharmacovigilance protect patients. Packaging (blister packs with aluminium protect against moisture — important in Nigeria's humid climate) and labelling are also controlled.

topics.title: Sterile Products Manufacturing
topics.summary: Cleanrooms, sterilisation methods, aseptic processing, pyrogens and parenteral QC.

material.heading: Cleanrooms and sterilisation
material.body: Sterile products (injections, eye drops, infusions) must be free from viable microorganisms, particulates and pyrogens. Cleanrooms are classified by airborne particle counts (EU GMP grades A–D; ISO classes — grade A ≈ ISO 5 for aseptic filling zones under unidirectional (laminar) airflow; grade B background), with HEPA filtration, positive pressure cascades, gowning, and environmental monitoring (settle plates, contact plates, air sampling). Terminal sterilisation in the final container is preferred when the product tolerates it: moist heat (autoclave — 121 °C for 15 minutes; overkill cycles; biological indicator Geobacillus stearothermophilus), dry heat (160–180 °C — glassware; depyrogenation at 250 °C), ionising radiation (gamma — disposable devices), and ethylene oxide gas (heat-sensitive devices; toxic residues). Filtration through 0.22 µm membranes sterilises heat-labile solutions, followed by aseptic filling. Sterility assurance level (SAL) of 10⁻⁶ is the target for terminal sterilisation.

material.heading: Pyrogens and QC
material.body: Pyrogens (mainly bacterial endotoxins — lipopolysaccharides from Gram-negative bacteria) cause fever when injected; they survive autoclaving and are removed by dry heat depyrogenation or controlled by using Water for Injection (WFI — produced by distillation or equivalent, stored hot at > 70 °C or circulated). Tests: bacterial endotoxin test (Limulus amoebocyte lysate — LAL; recombinant factor C alternatives) and the rabbit pyrogen test (historical). Parenteral QC: sterility test (membrane filtration or direct inoculation — 14 days), particulate matter (visible and sub-visible), container–closure integrity, pH and osmolarity (isotonicity — 0.9% NaCl), fill volume, and endotoxins. Media fill (process simulation) validates aseptic processing. Large-volume parenterals (infusions) are produced in Nigeria by several manufacturers; quality failures can cause serious harm (e.g. contaminated infusions causing sepsis).

topics.title: Good Manufacturing Practice and Quality Systems
topics.summary: GMP principles, documentation, validation, quality assurance vs control, and regulatory inspection.

material.heading: GMP principles
material.body: Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) ensures products are consistently produced and controlled to quality standards appropriate to their intended use. WHO GMP (adopted by NAFDAC) covers: quality management (pharmaceutical quality system, quality risk management — ICH Q9), personnel (qualified, trained, hygiene), premises and equipment (design to prevent contamination and mix-ups; cleaning validation), documentation ('if it isn't written down, it didn't happen' — specifications, master formulae, batch manufacturing records, SOPs; ALCOA+ data integrity principles: attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original, accurate), production (line clearance, segregation), quality control, complaints and recalls, self-inspection and contract manufacture. The 'authorised person' or qualified person releases batches. Quality assurance (QA — the whole system ensuring quality, preventing errors) is broader than quality control (QC — testing samples and materials). Deviations and out-of-specification results are investigated with CAPA (corrective and preventive actions).

material.heading: Validation and regulation
material.body: Validation provides documented evidence that a process, method, equipment or system consistently produces results meeting predetermined specifications. Qualification of equipment: design (DQ), installation (IQ), operational (OQ) and performance (PQ). Process validation (prospective — three consecutive batches traditionally; lifecycle approach), cleaning validation (acceptance limits for residues), analytical method validation (ICH Q2: accuracy, precision, specificity, linearity, range, detection and quantitation limits, robustness) and computer system validation. Change control manages modifications. Regulators: NAFDAC inspects and licenses manufacturers; WHO prequalification enables supply to global programmes (a few Nigerian manufacturers have achieved WHO prequalification, e.g. for zinc/ORS and antimalarials). The ICH guidelines (Q1 stability, Q7 APIs, Q8–Q10 development and quality systems) harmonise standards. Pharmaceutical inspection conventions (PIC/S) set inspection standards.

topics.title: Stability, Packaging and the Nigerian Pharmaceutical Industry
topics.summary: Drug stability and ICH conditions, packaging, and local manufacturing context.

material.heading: Stability
material.body: Drug degradation pathways: hydrolysis (esters — aspirin; amides; β-lactams), oxidation (catecholamines — adrenaline; vitamin C; prevented with antioxidants and nitrogen flushing), photolysis (light-sensitive drugs — nifedipine, riboflavin — amber containers), and physical instability (polymorphic changes, caking of suspensions, cracking of emulsions, moisture uptake). Reaction kinetics: zero-order (suspensions) and first-order (most solutions); shelf life (t90 — time to 90% potency). Accelerated stability testing (40 °C/75% RH for 6 months) predicts shelf life using the Arrhenius equation. ICH climatic zones: Nigeria is in Zone IVb (hot and very humid — long-term testing at 30 °C/75% RH), so products must be tested under these conditions. In-use stability, storage instructions ('store below 30 °C, protect from light and moisture') and cold chain for biologicals and vaccines are important.

material.heading: Local industry
material.body: Nigeria has over 100 pharmaceutical manufacturers (e.g. Emzor, Fidson, May & Baker, Swiss Pharma, Neimeth), concentrated in Lagos and the South-West, producing mainly generic solid and liquid dosage forms, infusions and some antimalarials; yet the country imports most active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs, largely from India and China) and many finished products. Challenges: dependence on imported APIs and excipients, foreign exchange scarcity, unreliable power (high cost of diesel generators), infrastructure, counterfeit competition and limited research capacity. Initiatives: local API production projects (e.g. Emzor's API plant), backward integration policy, Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Group of MAN (PMG-MAN), the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) opportunities, and vaccine manufacturing ambitions (e.g. Biovaccines Nigeria). The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted supply chain vulnerabilities and the need for local manufacturing and regulatory strengthening (NAFDAC achieved WHO Maturity Level 3 in 2022).
